sentences.text: Ultrastenos was a small crocodilian measuring upwards of 1.5 meters in length, possessing a flattened and short snout contrary to earlier proposals that it was elongated.

The external nostrils were positioned very close to the tip of its snout, giving the premaxilla a steep profile, and were longer than wide, opening slightly forward rather than straight up unlike many semi-aquatic crocodilians.

The nasal bones extended across the snout and touched the nostrils, while prominent teardrop-shaped supratemporal openings appeared in the skull; adult specimens possessed four premaxillary teeth, though the exact number of lower jaw teeth remains unknown despite suggestions of a minimum of 16.
The tibia differed from modern crocodiles by being flattened front-to-back and having a shaft that became more square further from the hip.
The genus Ultrastenos was described in 2016 based on a holotype specimen found at the Low Lion Site of the Riversleigh World Heritage Area, though fossils are also known from the White Hunter Site.

The holotype skull of the species previously known as Baru huberi measures approximately 20 cm in length and 11 cm in width, while Stephen Wroe estimated the total body length of that animal to be around 1.5 meters; the fossil material used to establish the genus measured 16 to 18 cm wide between the quadrates and approximately 35 cm in length.

Ultrastenos is believed to have been a semi-aquatic generalist with a broad, platyrostral skull, similar to Baru wickeni, likely inhabiting forest lakes and ponds drained by karstic limestone during the Late Oligocene when the Low Lion Site was covered by open forests lacking extensive river systems or wetlands.

The type species of Ultrastenos was originally designated as Ultrastenos willisi, while the species Ultrastenos huberi was originally described as a subdivision of the genus; due to priority rules, the valid species name is Ultrastenos huberi, honoring Professor Huber.
Stein et al. (2016) classified Ultrastenos as a mekosuchine crocodilian and a sister taxon to Trilophosuchus rackhami, with the parent group of Ultrastenos being Mekosuchinae.

Rio and Mannion published a study in 2021 discussing the phylogenetic position of Ultrastenos, while Lee and Yates (2018) recovered "Baru" huberi as closely related to the Bullock Creek taxon and Ristevski et al. (2023) found a clade linking "Baru" huberi and dwarf mekosuchines, excluding Quinkana.
Ultrastenos lived during the Chattian stage, from 27.3 to 23.04 million years ago.

It is debated whether Ultrastenos had a slender snout, as Stein and colleagues initially proposed that it was a longirostrine animal with jaws long and narrow like modern gharials, yet later studies suggest the initial interpretation of a narrow mandible was a misinterpretation and the animal actually had a more generalized lower jaw.

Willis previously considered Ultrastenos and Baru to be the same genus, using skull features to distinguish between them, but research suggests that the fossils of Ultrastenos and the previously named species Baru huberi belong to the same animal.
It is debated whether certain cranial fossils belong to Ultrastenos or to the species Baru wickeni, with some researchers proposing they belong to a juvenile Baru wickeni.
Researchers suggested that a re-description of the taxon was necessary following the discovery of related forms.
It is hypothesized that the development of slender jaws in mekosuchines may have been prevented by developmental constraints similar to those in alligators.
Some researchers suggest that Harpacochampsa may be a gavialoid, which affects the phylogenetic placement of related taxa.
It is debated whether the fossils at the White Hunter Site were transported after death (thanatocoenosis) or represent true sympatry.
